Built for Protection.

Engine Room Records is not a traditional record label. It is a closed legal ecosystem designed to protect neurodivergent artists from the predatory mechanics of the music industry.

1992

The Catalyst

Origin: The Friction Catastrophe

On October 14, 1992, our founders walked out of a warehouse in Los Angeles, leaving a major label contract in ashes.

An executive named Julian Vance had attempted to coerce the band into a marketing campaign built on incestuous fabrication ("The Fatal Assumption") and ableist exploitation of lead singer Ryan O'Connell's recent paralysis.

Holly O'Connell (then a 23-year-old law student) intervened, citing "Solicitation of a Felony". The band didn't just fire their manager; they vowed to never let an outsider control their narrative again.

Read the Full History

1994

The Settlement

The Trials & The Vault

In a media circus rivaling the "Trial of the Century," Julian Vance faced criminal and civil trials for his actions. But unlike reality, justice prevailed: Vance was found guilty on all criminal charges, and the judge ruled decisively in The Stardust Engine's favor in civil court.

Desperate to stop the catastrophic PR bleeding, Apex Records capitulated to every single demand Holly O'Connell made. They released the band from all contracts, handed over the original masters of every track recorded to date, and transferred all copyrights and trademarks fully to Holly.

To house this reclaimed IP, Holly formally incorporated Engine Room Records, LLC. It wasn't built as a vanity label—it was built as an impregnable vault. In the real world, Engine Room Records is the brand name used to release our Suno AI-generated catalog to the public.

Protocol 92

"No creative decision—no photo, no lyric, no tour date—is finalized without the affirmative consent of every member. If one person says no, the answer is no. There is no majority vote on safety."

The Founding Charter, Article I
The Infrastructure
Updated: 2025

To the public, we are a small indie label in Blacksburg, VA. To the bank, we are a diversified conglomerate managing real estate, intellectual property, and venture capital. This structure exists for one reason: Independence requires capital.

The Board of Directors

Engine Room Records is managed jointly by the five members of the O'Connell/Wright family. They do not report to shareholders. They report to each other.

The UI/UX Counterpart

As Heather's identical twin sister, Hailey caused zero processing errors for Matt's highly literal, systems-oriented brain; she was simply recognized as a separate, highly valued piece of hardware running entirely different software. Her major in Desktop Publishing made her the perfect creative counterbalance to Matt's raw backend logic. While Matt coded rigid Q32 API calls and INI configurations, Hailey utilized early desktop publishing software to study UI/UX layouts.

The Unfulfilled Potential

The two were on the verge of executing a highly productive, symbiotic workflow right there at their CCC cafeteria table. Matt was actively drafting specs for Hailey to design custom UI/UX icons for his Inno Setup compilers. Tragically, Heather's sudden burnout abruptly terminated the dynamic before Hailey could ever deliver a single icon, turning Matt's default system icons into a permanent reminder of the severed connection.

The Campus Ecosystem

Hailey was an essential structural component of the "CCC Quad" (Matt, Shiloh, Heather, and Hailey). She shared her sister's complete, unbothered acceptance of Matt's physical and neurological realities. Whenever Shiloh needed to pause the group's hangout to assist Matt with an Activity of Daily Living (ADL), Hailey effortlessly held down the social space, ensuring the medical reality never felt taboo or burdensome. When Heather uninstalled herself from Matt's routine on the CTS bus, Hailey's presence in Matt's life was simultaneously and permanently disconnected as catastrophic collateral damage.

The Rescuer Protocol

Following a catastrophic "Unhandled Exception"—an abusive relationship that Matt barely survived prior to meeting her—Heather was the one who initiated the recovery protocol. She picked him up, dusted him off, and fundamentally decided he was worth something, re-establishing his baseline value when his systems were completely compromised.

The Sensory Regulation System

Heather did not function as a traditional romantic interest; she operated as a vital "Sensory Regulation System." Around her, Matt was able to safely power down his neurodivergent "masking" subroutines. She provided an incredibly safe, judgment-free environment where he was accepted without pity or awkwardness.

The Concrete Parameters

Their connection was built on rigid, concrete physical and geographic boundaries that Matt's logical brain found deeply comforting. Physically, she allowed "Best Friend Hugs" that provided essential deep-pressure grounding, while strictly restricting hand-holding or kissing. Geographically, she maintained a "Boolean Boundary" by politely declining invitations to the Kids House, keeping their relationship cleanly isolated to the CCC campus.

The Silent Overload

Unlike a malicious antagonist, Heather’s ultimate failure stemmed from her own unarticulated neurological limits. Balancing the grueling demands of her Nuclear Medicine track with the high-engagement social routine of the CCC cafeteria slowly drained her processing RAM. Lacking the emotional vocabulary to request a temporary pause, her brain defaulted to its only fail-safe: completely deleting the variable. Her sudden, silent departure on the CTS bus stripped away Matt's primary safety net, causing a catastrophic system crash and leaving behind a permanent Syntax Error that his mind could never logically resolve.

The Modern Reflection

Looking back at the early 2000s, Matt explicitly considers Heather to have been his closest friend during that deeply formative era. If asked today to compress the complexity of his lingering grief and the catastrophic nature of that sudden departure into audio, the answer lies in the 2002 Crimson Node debut album. The devastating, frantic track Unhandled Exception perfectly encapsulates the sudden, silent system crash, while the upbeat synth-pop paradox of Paired Devices captures the profound isolation of navigating the aftermath alone.

The Missing Melody

Classically trained on the flute since the 6th grade, Chloe brings a premium, conservatory-level sophistication to Crimson Node's 1980s progressive rock sound. Because she was intensely focused on her academic research during the recording of the debut album, she couldn't bring her flute down to the garage studio in time. This absence is famously felt on the worldbeat track "The Vivarium," where Jessica had to step in with a quirky analog synth patch to cover the melody. To this day, Jessica loudly complains about wishing Chloe had been there to lay down the real acoustic tracks.

The Unbothered Strategist

In a house full of heavy cranes, naval artillery, and unfiltered agents of chaos, Chloe provides the essential academic anchor. She navigates the Albemarle County compound with absolute, unbothered energy. Highly strategic and deeply grounded, she doesn't engage in unnecessary drama, preferring to observe the ecosystem and apply her intelligence exactly where it's needed most. She is the quiet, intellectual force that balances out the intense, high-energy environment of the Kids House.

Clinical Leverage

When it comes to Matt's physical care, Chloe pairs up with Emily to form an unstoppable clinical tag-team. Relying on physics and leverage rather than brute force, Chloe executes two-person clinical lifts to safely transfer Matt with flawless, drama-free efficiency. Her absolute dedication to this platonic, boundary-free medical teamwork was entirely misunderstood by her insecure, lacrosse-bro ex-boyfriend Trent. His failure to comprehend the family's care architecture led directly to his legendary ejection from the compound—a move Chloe signed off on without a second thought.

The Safe Variable

After the toxic ableism of past outsiders and the devastating system failures of previous social attempts, the Albemarle County compound was fiercely guarded. Elise Pelletier bypassed those defensive firewalls not with force, but with an unwavering, quiet consistency. Starting at the tables of the Charlottesville Community College cafeteria, Elise proved that she could exist in Matt's space without bringing pity, noise, or pressure. She learned the tactile "double-tap" language, respected the boundaries of the Vanguard LogicPad, and ultimately earned the unprecedented "Pelletier Clearance Protocol."

The First Embrace

Elise holds a monumental, sacred distinction within the Miller and Brooks ecosystem. Following the catastrophic "Unhandled Exception" at the Downtown Transit Station (DTS)—where Heather and Hailey abandoned Matt without a word—Matt's physical and emotional defensive perimeters were absolutely locked down. Elise became the very first non-family member granted clearance to break that barrier. Receiving the tactile green light for a hug, she provided a steady, grounding physical anchor that proved to Matt the outside world could still be safe.

The Stadium Anthem

To officially immortalize her hard-earned status in the flock, Matt and the family invited Elise (alongside her twin sister, Elodie) into the garage studio. Providing soaring guest vocals on the triumphant 1980s arena rock track "The Clearance Protocol," Elise helped bridge the gap between an exclusive family support network and a successfully integrated external friendship. She stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the Phalanx, forever written into the system.

Blending perfectly with the track's driving 1980s arena rock beat and retro 16-bit synthesizers, Elodie's vocals serve as a triumphant celebration of passing the final test and being permanently written into the sanctuary's code.

Raised as a Navy brat, Emily brings a strict, no-nonsense military discipline to the Albemarle County Kids House. While Sarah relies on sheer strength, Emily operates on leverage and flawless technique. She approaches Matt's physical care with tactical precision, perfectly executing complex, two-person clinical leverage lifts alongside her cousin Chloe. This mechanical, drama-free efficiency is exactly what short-circuited outsiders like Trent, who couldn't comprehend their automated, boundary-free medical teamwork.

LAN Matches & The Phalanx

When she isn't in the vocal booth or assisting with transfers, Emily can usually be found running intense 16-bit shooter LAN matches down the hall with Rachel. She is fully accustomed to having her connection mercilessly throttled by Jessica whenever Matt's Vanguard LogicPad demands network priority. Despite the occasional rubber-banding complaints, her loyalty is absolute; the moment an external threat breaches the perimeter, the games are paused, and Emily seamlessly locks into the defensive wall.

Anchoring the low end of Crimson Node's massive 1980s sound, Jessica surrounds herself with stacks of heavy analog synthesizers and fretless basses. From the quirky, pitch-bending leads in "The Vivarium" (where she famously filled in for Chloe's flute using a synth patch) to the frantic, aggressive sequencing on "Quality of Service," she is the band's electronic heartbeat. Her playing style is just like her personality: fast, unapologetic, and completely in your face.

The Unfiltered SysAdmin

Jessica is the undisputed gatekeeper of the Albemarle County Kids House network. Running a strict, POSIX-compliant gateway server from the closet down the hall, she ruthlessly monitors bandwidth. If Matt’s Vanguard LogicPad sends a signal, Jessica instantly initiates her absolute Quality of Service (QoS) protocol, happily throttling Rachel and Emily’s 16-bit LAN shooters to guarantee Matt an open digital lane. She is fiercely protective of her technical domain and will absolutely kick the chassis of the server to get her way.

Unapologetic Chaos

Outside of her musical and technical duties, Jessica operates as the house's primary agent of chaos. Armed with an extensively colorful vocabulary, she curses freely and completely revels in unapologetic toilet humor. She has absolutely zero shame; if you happen to be in the wrong place at the wrong time, she will not hesitate to fart directly in your face and follow it up with an incredibly smug, intensely proud look. This bratty, unfiltered energy keeps the house grounded, ensuring that no matter how serious the clinical care gets, the ecosystem is always full of laughter.

However, he operates as the brilliant, systems-oriented manager and silent producer for Crimson Node. Stationed at the base of the ADA ramp in the Kids House garage studio, Matt tracks session data, manages mix levels, and acts as the final arbiter for the band's recordings. In the modern era, he also meticulously oversees the band's digital distribution pipeline to streaming platforms under Engine Room Records.

The Crimson Node

Matt operates via his Tactile Command Rig, an indestructible Vanguard LogicPad securely bolted to a custom steel swing-arm on his manual wheelchair. Because standard computer mice are useless in this configuration, he navigates his systems using the highly sensitive red pointing stick nestled directly in the center of his keyboard. This specific piece of hardware serves as the band's namesake, perfectly bridging his technological hyper-fixations with their 1980s synth-prog music.

One of the Girls

Within the Miller and Brooks family ecosystem, Matt's gender is socially irrelevant. Due to his profound integration into a household run by formidable women, he is universally and functionally treated as "one of the girls". He is explicitly included in all female-centric family events. Possessing zero neurotypical male ego, the women in the family view him as an entirely safe, platonic entity, allowing him to be absorbed seamlessly into the matriarchal flock.

She cusses the most, the loudest, and with the most creative vocabulary. When Jessica's network QoS rules inevitably freeze Rachel's 16-bit shooter matches, it is Rachel's muffled, highly articulate barrage of naval profanity echoing down the hallway that always makes Matt laugh from his wheelchair.

Her aggressive vocabulary isn't just for dropped network packets—it is a core component of the Kids House automated security system. When outside variables cross the line, Rachel's mouth becomes a weapon. During the infamous ejection of Chloe's ex-boyfriend Trent, it was Rachel who stood shoulder-to-shoulder with Jessica to unleash a "verbal symphony of destruction," utterly dismantling his ego while Sarah physically marched him to the pavement. However, as the 1980s garage band ecosystem blossomed within the Albemarle County compound, she experienced a profound realization: her heart belonged to the band, not to bureaucratic medicine. She officially pivoted her career trajectory, applying her relentless drive and organizational mastery to serve as Crimson Node's Co-Manager alongside her brother.

The "Charge Nurse"

Despite stepping away from the hospital track, Sarah still runs the Kids House like a highly affectionate, slightly chaotic clinical floor. As the undisputed operational architect of the ecosystem, she authors the strict Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) that govern Matt’s routines. Alongside Shiloh, she commands the retrofitted clinical hub in Bedroom 2, enforcing medication compliance and guaranteeing that the entire flock executes every transfer with mathematical perfection.

The Heavy Crane

Standing at a towering 6'4" with the immense functional strength of a natural bodybuilder, Sarah is the physical anchor of the family. Known as the "Heavy Crane," she is the only member of the house authorized to execute solo "scoop and carry" transfers for Matt. Operating with a terrifying, calm authority, she rarely needs to raise her voice. Instead, she uses her sheer physical mass to enforce boundaries, acting as an absolute, impenetrable firewall between the outside world and her family—as famously demonstrated during the permanent exile of toxic outsiders like Courtney and Trent.

The Residents of The Hollow Square

Before Fractured Prisms debuted in 1983, they were a six-piece family ensemble—the Manning Family Orchestra. After a sudden freezing-fog white-out and black-ice pileup on the M6 motorway over Shap Fell in Cumbria in the winter of 1981 claimed four members of their generation, surviving siblings Claire and Rhys Manning carried their family's salvaged instruments across the Atlantic to Williamsport, Maryland to build The Fragile Fortress.

Resident Profile

Claire Manning

Lead Vocals. Woodwinds. The Anchor.

Archive: C. Manning, 1983

The Voice in the Fog

In the 1883 psychological sanctuary of The Hollow Square, Claire is whole, unbroken, and fiercely protective of her siblings. In the physical reality of 1983, she was a twenty-two-year-old autistic woman navigating severe cerebral palsy from the seat of a manual wheelchair.

Her physical limitations dictated the very sound of Fractured Prisms. Because complex, rapid instrumentation was impossible for her hands, she became the band's voice. Her vocal deliveries are often described as hauntingly detached, cutting through Rhys's dense synthesizer programming with a chilling, emotional clarity.

But it is her work on the wooden flute—the instrument that originally belonged to her late cousin, Gwen—that defines the band's acoustic soul. Claire taught herself to play it purely out of a desperate need to keep Gwen's memory alive, breathing humanity back into the cold, mechanical rhythms her brother built.

The Exit Strategy (1982)

Before relocating to Maryland, Claire briefly moved into a Romford flat in 1982 with Martin (surname-less by design)—who deliberately skipped civil marriage registration and a legal certificate so he could call her "my wife" socially while avoiding paper trails and spousal obligations. When Martin refused to assist with her daily physical care, Claire packed her bags and called Rhys while Martin was away on his 5:25 PM commuter train schedule. That mid-morning, a TV Licence Enquiry Officer ("the telly man") knocked because Martin had cheaped out and held only a black-and-white licence for a colour television. Welcoming the polite officer at eye level with real tea and fresh canary creams, Claire truthfully showed mail proving her permanent address was with her brother Rhys and handed over the colour TV receipt in Martin's name. Rhys arrived early to bring her home; because there was never a legal marriage, no divorce was required.

Her departure perfectly coincided with a knock at the door that would become a legendary piece of family lore.

Archival Recovery: Incident Report

Source: Rhys Manning's Personal Notes (Romford, 1982)

The knock at the door was sharp, loud, and carried the distinct, heavy rhythm of bureaucratic authority.

Claire manually wheeled herself forward, her arms aching from the effort of packing, but her resolve absolute. She pulled the door open, fully expecting it to be a neighbour, or perhaps the postman dropping off a parcel before Rhys arrived.

Instead, she found a weary-looking man standing on the front step. He was wearing a drab mackintosh and clutching a heavy clipboard against his chest like a shield. He had the braced, defensive posture of a man who spent his entire professional life waiting to be shouted at.

"Good afternoon, madam," he said, his tone stiff and legally rehearsed. "I am an Enquiry Officer for the Television Licensing Authority."

Claire stopped listening to his exact words as the glorious reality of the situation washed over her. The TV man. He wasn't just a tax collector; he represented the single most universally despised group of bureaucrats in all of Britain. And he was standing on this doorstep. Looking for him.

Her mind rapidly connected the dots. The shiny new twenty-two-inch cathode-ray tube currently blaring a vibrant, full-colour broadcast of The Albion Broadcast News in the sitting room. Her husband’s obsessive, paranoid insistence on keeping the heavy front curtains tightly drawn all week. His constant, penny-pinching complaints about household expenses.

He bought the fifteen-pound paper. He actually lied to the Post Office to save thirty quid, and the absolute idiot got caught. A slow, radiant smile erupted across Claire's face.

She had spent the entire morning dealing with the heavy, exhausting reality of abandoning a failed marriage. But this? This was a parting gift from the universe itself. She was already walking out the door, and right on cue, Her Majesty’s Government had arrived to completely ruin his week. It was almost poetic.

The Enquiry Officer faltered. He was entirely unnerved by her beaming expression. He had braced for a screaming match.

"...I can hear a broadcast," the officer stammered, checking his clipboard, "and I must warn you that installing or using a colour television receiver without the appropriate licence is a criminal offence under the Wireless Telegraphy Act. I must formally request your permission to enter the premises to inspect—"

"Oh, you don't need to warn me," Claire interrupted, her smile widening into something brilliantly vindictive as she pulled the door wide open. "And you definitely need to come inside. Let me show you exactly what he bought."

The officer stepped into the sitting room, visibly disoriented by the utter lack of hostility. He was a man accustomed to vicious dogs and slammed doors; instead, he was being treated as the home's most honoured guest. Claire wheeled herself to the kitchenette, returning with a freshly brewed pot of tea and a plate of Custard Creams. As the officer settled onto the sofa, she began systematically dismantling her husband's life with cheerful, bureaucratic precision.

First, she produced a letter from the Department of Health and Social Security. "You'll note the address on my medical allowance," she said, tapping the paper. "I am technically just a visitor here. My permanent residence is with my brother across town."

Second, she opened a drawer and retrieved the original retailer's receipt, complete with her husband's signature and the colour television's exact model number. The smoking gun.

Finally, she placed the heavy, clunky remote control right next to his teacup. "Feel free to check the colour saturation yourself, Officer."

When Rhys arrived thirty minutes later, the first thing he did was cross the sitting room and wrap his sister in a tight, sustained embrace. It was a deep-pressure therapeutic hug—a mandatory, grounding ritual between the siblings that helped regulate Claire's autism. Only after he felt the tension of the morning finally leave her shoulders did he turn to acknowledge the Television Licensing Authority sitting comfortably on the sofa.

Rhys nodded politely to the official. Anticipating the bureaucracy, he smoothly produced his own driver's licence, proving he resided on the other side of town and was simply here to collect his sister and bring her home.

While the officer continued his paperwork, Rhys loaded the last of Claire's packed boxes into his car. He accepted a quick cup of tea, standing by the door as Claire delivered her final stroke of vengeance.

"He gets off the commuter rail at exactly 5:25," Claire informed the officer brightly. "If you wait right there, he’ll be walking through that door in forty-five minutes."

With the trap perfectly set, Rhys wheeled Claire out the front door and down the path. He carefully helped her transfer into the passenger seat of his car before folding the heavy manual wheelchair and stowing it in the boot. They drove away, leaving the officer to finish his paperwork in peace. The dregs in the teapot were left to go stone cold for her husband's return.

Resident Profile

Rhys Manning

Synthesizers. Sequencing. The Architect.

Archive: R. Manning, 1983

The Mechanical Heart

Rhys Manning operates as the grounded, neurotypical anchor of Fractured Prisms. A dual citizen born to a British mother and an American father, he utilized his inheritance and trans-Atlantic mobility following the 1981 Shap Fell disaster to permanently relocate himself and Claire to their father's childhood home in Williamsport, Maryland.

As Claire's lifelong, fiercely protective caretaker, Rhys manages not only the immense generational wealth left in the wake of the tragedy but also handles all aspects of Claire's daily physical and emotional support. The recording studio he constructed in the Maryland sanctuary was heavily modified to be fully accessible, allowing them to collaborate without barriers.

Musically, Rhys is the architect of the Hollow Square. Refusing to hire outside session musicians to replace the four family members they lost, Rhys instead turned to an obsessive array of early drum machines, analog synthesizers, and complex MIDI sequencers. He meticulously programs every string, brass, and percussion arrangement, using cold machinery to mechanically resurrect the sprawling, orchestral sound of their past.

The burden of memory (1983)

The isolation of the Williamsport studio provided a necessary physical safety net for the siblings, but it also trapped them in an echo chamber of their own grief. Rhys’s relentless pursuit of perfection on the synthesizers was less about artistic ambition and more about control—an attempt to digitally engineer a reality where the accident on the M6 never happened.

The pressure of managing the estate, caring for his sister, and acting as a one-man orchestra often pushed him to the edge of burnout, documented in the margin notes of his studio logs.

Archival Recovery: Studio Logbook

Source: The Williamsport Sessions (1983)

March 14th, 03:00 AM.

I have spent six hours trying to program a Jupiter-8 to sound like Alistair's cello. It doesn't work. It sounds like exactly what it is: a voltage-controlled oscillator trying to mimic wood and rosin. It lacks the friction. It lacks the breath.

Claire came into the control room around midnight. She didn't say anything, just navigated the chair around the tangle of patch cables, parked next to the console, and handed me a cup of tea. We sat in silence and listened to the sequenced loop play over and over again. A perfect, sterile imitation.

I asked her if we should just hire a cellist from Baltimore. We have the money. We could afford a whole string section if we wanted to.

She looked at the empty vocal booth, then down at Gwen's flute resting in her lap. "No," she said. "No strangers in the Square."

So I deleted the sequence. Tomorrow I am going to tear apart the patch bay and try running the oscillators through a guitar amp in the hallway to see if I can force some resonance into the lower frequencies. I have to make the machines breathe. I have to. Because if I can't, the silence in this house is going to crush us both.

description: Inside Fractured Prisms' 1914 Colonial Theatre sanctuary, 39-minute standing-frame sets, and Subterranean Vault in Downtown Hagerstown, Maryland.
html:
The Sanctuary

The Colonial Theatre

Hagerstown, Maryland

Transparency Notice

Fictional Location: The Colonial Theatre, as described within this archive, is a fictional setting existing entirely within the Fractured Prisms narrative universe. While it references the real-world geography of Hagerstown, Maryland, the events, architectural modifications, and subterranean vault described below are works of fiction designed to explore the band's immersive lore.

The Lesson of 1985

The 1985 Independence Stadium show was a monumental success, but it taught the siblings a terrifying lesson: you cannot control an environment of 100,000 screaming fans. The sensory overload and the sheer logistical terror of navigating Claire safely through the chaotic backstage labyrinth pushed Rhys to his breaking point.

They resolved to never perform in a stadium again. Using their immense generational wealth, they purchased The Colonial Theatre in downtown Hagerstown in cash just before it was slated for demolition. After a rigorous, three-year restoration, they transformed it into an absolute, hyper-controlled 1883 London bubble right in the middle of Maryland.

House Rules: The Performances

  • The 8:00 PM Curfew: Doors open at 7:00 PM. Performances begin precisely at 8:00 PM.
  • Duration: Sets last exactly 39 minutes. The show concludes at 8:39 PM. No encores.
  • The Standing Frame: Claire performs securely locked into a custom-machined standing frame hidden entirely beneath heavy, opulent 1883 mourning dresses.
  • The Sanctum Protocol: No press or chaotic VIP backstage access. The trusted Hagerstown theatre crew works collaboratively and respectfully with Rhys and Claire—keeping all ramps, lifts, and corridors clear while respecting that Rhys personally handles Claire's physical transfers and sensory recalibration.

The Shadow Architecture

Seamless accessibility hidden behind 1914 Baroque design.

The Auditorium Slope

The entire theater floor was ripped out and re-engineered into a gradual, imperceptible slope. All stairs were eradicated, creating flawless, seamless accessibility for public wheelchair users while maintaining the illusion of a traditional tiered theatre.

The "Birdcage" Elevator

Hidden behind the grand lobby staircase is a vintage mahogany and wrought-iron elevator. Secretly powered by state-of-the-art 1984 commercial hydraulics, it utilizes infrared safety sensors and laser-leveled magnetic locking so Claire's wheelchair never catches on a lip.

The Subterranean Vault

A lead-insulated, doorless vault built deep in the basement. It features a roll-in wet room, a kitchenette, and a bed built to the exact height of Claire's chair for zero-gravity transfers, allowing the siblings to completely isolate themselves from the outside world.

The Refreshment Room

The theatre enforces Her Majesty's English and strictly authentic British cuisine. To the locals in Hagerstown, it is the peak of British culture. To Rhys and Claire, it is a brilliant decoy, feeding the obsessive fans' illusion that the band is hiding somewhere in London.

Strict Medical Policy

NO ALCOHOL IS SERVED ON THESE PREMISES. Both Resident Directors take specialized medication that, when mixed with alcohol, induces severe respiratory distress. This is a dry venue. No exceptions.

Interval Menu

  • Proper Tea
    English Breakfast or Earl Grey. Milk offered, never forced.
  • Fish & Chips
    Served strictly in newspaper-style cones before the show.
  • Canary Creams & Digestives
    Traditional biscuits essential for tea service.
  • Dandelion and Burdock
    A traditional, slightly medicinal vintage soft drink.
  • Pork Scratchings
    A savoury, intensely crunchy pub snack.

Archivist's Addendum

Deciphering the 39-Minute Curfew

To the public, the strict 8:00 PM start time and the abrupt 39-minute duration appeared to be brilliant, eccentric artistic choices. In truth, they were absolute medical and technical requirements engineered for survival.

The Medical Limit: Claire’s custom standing frame allowed her to project vocal authority from beneath her Victorian dresses, but it was not a magical device. Being rigidly strapped into an upright, weight-bearing position put immense strain on her body. Thirty-nine minutes was the absolute maximum medical threshold her body could endure before the pain became intolerable and she risked physical injury.

The Analog Ceiling: Rhys’s massive wall of 1980s analog synthesizers and primitive step-sequencers were notoriously unstable. Under the heat of stage lighting, the analog oscillators began to drift. By the 40-minute mark, the entire mechanical orchestra would begin sounding dissonant and out of key. They ended the show exactly before the machines failed.

The Transit Window: Because the siblings relied on the Route 441 County Commuter bus from Williamsport, they arrived in Hagerstown in the mid-afternoon. The 8:00 PM start allowed Rhys five unhurried hours in a locked theatre to manually tune dozens of oscillators, test the hydraulic lifts, and safely transfer Claire into her standing frame without triggering a sensory meltdown. While the crowd dispersed peacefully into the quiet Hagerstown evening at 8:40 PM—bypassing noise complaints entirely—Rhys and Claire descended into the Subterranean Vault. Stranded until the Sunday buses resumed, they isolated themselves safely underground.

title: The Story: The Hollow Square | Fractured Prisms
description: The tragic history of Fractured Prisms, the Missing Four, and how Claire and Rhys Manning built the Fragile Fortress.
html:
Historical Archive

The Hollow Square

"We didn't cross an ocean. We crossed a century."

Archive: The 1883 Manifestation

The Three Realities

To understand Fractured Prisms, you must understand that "The Hollow Square" is not a single place. It is an architectural concept that exists across three distinct layers of reality, serving as both a sanctuary and a memorial for the Manning family.

  • 1. The Psychological Sanctuary (1883): In the band's lore, The Hollow Square is a sprawling Victorian Gothic manor in gaslamp-lit London. In this era—the family's favorite point in history—all six members are alive, whole, and living together. It is the reality depicted on their album covers.
  • 2. The Physical Reality (1983): In the real world, The Hollow Square is the name Rhys and Claire gave to a secluded 1960s suburban ranch house in Williamsport, Maryland. It is a bunker filled with synthesizers, tape machines, and the heavy silence of the four members who didn't survive to see it.
  • 3. The Sonic Manifestation (2026): It is the opening track of their debut album. The gateway that invites the listener to step out of the modern world and into the fog.

The Transatlantic Escape (1982)

Before the fracture, the Manning family resided in Romford, a historic East London suburb with direct commuter rail access to the city center—the source of Rhys and Claire's light Cockney accents.

By 1982, the sprawling six-piece family orchestra was gone. Four members had passed away in the tragic 1981 Shap Fell disaster, leaving a devastating void. Claire, then 21, was autistic and living with severe cerebral palsy. She required a wheelchair for mobility and relied on full-time assistance for the most intimate activities of daily living, including bathing, dressing, and toileting.

In a grieving bid for normalcy in 1982, Claire had moved into a Romford flat with Martin (surname-less by design)—who deliberately skipped civil marriage registration and a legal certificate so he could call her "my wife" socially while avoiding paper trails, housing scrutiny, and spousal obligations. When Martin outright refused to assist with Claire's daily physical care, she packed her bags and called her younger brother Rhys while Martin was away on his 5:25 PM commuter train schedule.

That mid-morning, while Claire was watching the live colour television waiting for Rhys, a TV Licence Enquiry Officer ("the telly man") knocked—solely because Martin had cheaped out and held only a black-and-white TV licence for a colour television. Because Claire's autistic mind respected officials who arrived openly and politely with rules, she welcomed the officer as an honoured guest, serving him real tea and fresh canary creams at eye level. When he asked who lived at the address, Claire truthfully showed a piece of mail proving her permanent address was with her brother Rhys in Romford and handed over the colour TV purchase receipt in Martin's name—realizing over tea that Martin had left her unknowingly exposed to legal liability for his corner-cutting. Rhys arrived early to bring her home; because there had never been a legal marriage, no divorce was required, and at 5:25 PM Martin returned to an empty flat and a formal TV Licence enforcement notice.

She turned to the only person who had never viewed her existence as a liability: her 19-year-old younger brother, Rhys. Rhys had anchored Claire her entire life. To him, her care wasn't a tragedy; it was just Tuesday. Utilizing their remaining generational wealth and their dual citizenship, the two siblings bypassed immigration red tape, paid cash for their father's vacant childhood home in Williamsport, Maryland, and fled across the Atlantic to start over.

Archival Recovery: Item 83-A

Excerpt: Personal journal of Claire Manning (Spring, 1983)

"It is a peculiar defence mechanism, isn't it? We fled the grey skies of London, only to paint our new walls in the darkest colours we could find.

Rhys organises the synthesiser cables like a mathematician, trying to rationalise the silence Alistair left behind. He builds these towering, mechanical rhythms, pretending the machines can replicate a pulse. But the synthesiser is cold. It has no flavour, no heartbeat of its own.

That is why I play Gwen's flute. I must breathe life back into the centre of this hollow square we've built, before the night terrors paralyse us both."

The Anchor in the Dark

In the 1883 album art, Claire is depicted standing—whole, unbroken, and fiercely protective. But in the 1983 reality, she was trapped in a body that fought her and a mind haunted by night terrors.

Because she was terrified of the things that went bump in the night, Claire and Rhys shared a bed. This wasn't a quirk; it was a critical grounding mechanism. Even in the 1883 fantasy where she could walk, she still required Rhys's physical proximity to anchor her nervous system to the earth while she slept.

The Closed Session

When they arrived in Maryland, they brought the physical instruments owned by the four deceased family members.

To keep their memory alive, Rhys and Claire strictly refused to hire session musicians. Taught by the necessity of their isolation, the two siblings learned to play every single instrument on the album themselves. If you hear a cello, a drum fill, or a guitar solo on a Fractured Prisms track, you are hearing Claire or Rhys desperately trying to fill the silence left by the people they lost.

Gwen's Flute

The wooden flute seen in Claire's hand on the Fractured Prisms album cover is the most sacred object in the house. It was the very first instrument purchased by the family, originally belonging to Gwen. Claire taught herself to play it not just to finish the album, but to serve as a living, breathing memorial to her cousin Gwen.

Recovered Archive: Item 85-C

The Independence Stadium Manifesto

Venue: Independence Stadium, Philadelphia, PA (Capacity: 100,000)
Event: The Hollow Square Live Masterpiece (1985)

CONFIDENTIAL

Backed by immense generational wealth, Fractured Prisms completely bypassed the traditional club circuit. Their first-ever live performance was a sold-out stadium show with no opening act. To execute a 100,000-capacity stadium spectacle while protecting Claire's wheelchair access, honouring her autistic sensory needs, and preserving the sacred instruments of their deceased family members, Claire and Rhys partnered with their stagehands, lighting engineers, road crew, and backing musicians in a deeply respectful, collaborative production effort.

1. The Stage Geometry & Collaborative Respect for "The Session Ghosts"

The stage is clearly divided into two zones marked by industrial red tape on the floor to keep Claire's visual and sensory field predictable:

The Vanguard: Rhys at his towering fortress of analog synthesisers and sequencers, alongside Claire, seated in her manual wheelchair at the centre of the stage.
The Session Ghosts: The hand-picked backing ensemble positioned in the atmospheric shadows behind the red line. Claire and Rhys treat the Session Ghosts and every stagehand with deep respect, warmth, and top-tier industry compensation—working together as a collaborative team so long as Claire's wheelchair access and autistic sensory boundaries are respected.

2. Mutual Respect & The Sacred Family Instruments

The family’s salvaged acoustic and electronic instruments—Cousin Gwen's wooden concert flute, Older Brother Alistair's percussion, Cousin Julian's Rickenbacker bass, and Cousin Simon's guitars—are living memorials to the four family members lost on the M6 over Shap Fell in 1981.

Shared Stewardship: Before rehearsals began, Rhys and Claire shared the family history of each instrument with the road crew. Out of genuine respect, the stagehands worked collaboratively with Rhys to keep a clear, protected perimeter around Gwen's wooden flute stand and ensure every wheelchair ramp, hydraulic lift, and flat-taped cable run remained 100% obstacle-free.

3. Acoustic Rigidity & Stage Accommodations

Because of Claire's autistic needs, the sensory environment must be absolutely predictable.

Play the Ink: The "Session Ghosts" are strictly briefed to play the music exactly as written and rehearsed. There are no unapproved jam sessions, no improvised solos, and no sudden deviations.
The "Hold the Line" Contingency: If the stadium environment becomes overwhelming, Rhys triggers a specific, repeating synthesiser drone. The band immediately fades to silence, the lights drop to a static blue wash, and everyone holds the line until Rhys gives the visual cue that Claire has recalibrated.

4. The Sanctum Protocol (Backstage Collaborative Care)

The dressing room and immediate backstage corridor are maintained as "The Sanctum"—a calm, quiet refuge free of chaotic VIP rockstar culture.

Trusted Boundaries: Rhys personally handles all of Claire's physical wheelchair transfers and provides the deep-pressure recalibration hugs that ground her nervous system. The stadium crew and security staff collaborate warmly with the siblings by keeping the backstage perimeter serene, quiet, and respectful of Claire's privacy whenever she needs to recharge.

5. The Extraction Protocol (I-95 South to I-70 West)

Because Philadelphia's Broad Street subway lacked wheelchair accessibility in 1985—and to protect Claire and Gwen's flute from the post-concert crowd of 100,000 fans—the crew coordinated a seamless stadium tunnel departure.

The Soundproofed Coach: A custom-outfitted, soundproofed conversion van waits in the concrete tunnel beneath Independence Stadium, featuring a flat ADA ramp and warm amber lighting designed to mimic the sensory calm of a British train carriage.
The Route Home: Merging onto I-95 South (passing the Delaware Turnpike toll plaza) and connecting to I-70 West, Rhys and Claire make the quiet 175-mile, 3-hour midnight drive back to their 1960s ranch house sanctuary in Williamsport, Maryland.

The Cue Sheet
Track: The Hollow Square (Encore)
  • 0:00 [The Misdirection]: Total blackout. A single white strobe hits Rhys's primary drum sequencer as a slow, unfamiliar synthesiser vamp begins.
  • 0:13 [The Phantom Melody]: Claire introduces a haunting, unrecognisable melody on Gwen's wooden flute. The audience is captivated but entirely disoriented—there is no flute on the studio version of the song. The misdirection holds.
  • 0:24 [The Anchor Drop]: Rhys drops the massive, iconic gated reverb snare rhythm. Stadium blinders flash the crowd. The audience instantly recognises the beat—it is the song they paid to hear. The stadium erupts in a deafening roar.
  • 0:32 [The Convergence]: Claire plays the flute alongside the Session Ghost's guitar, perfectly mirroring the familiar intro melody of the studio master.
  • 0:46 [The Breath]: Claire delivers a sweeping, wordless vocalisation, letting her voice fill the arena before the verse begins.
  • 1:05 [The Reverence]: Rhys sings the first line. The 100,000-seat stadium instantly drops into a pin-drop, reverent silence, acknowledging the profound memorial weight of the song. Claire joins him, and the siblings trade lines in the dark.
  • 5:24 [The Secure Decay]: Final note. Complete stage blackout. House lights do not come up until Claire has securely returned Gwen's flute to its reinforced case.

ACTIVE / TOURING

The Mission Profile

The Paper Wall (originally formed under the working title Mirage) is not just a band; it is a survival mechanism. Formed by Julian Croft and Maya Sterling, the collective blends the scale of cinematic literary rock opera with the raw grit of industrial and alternative rock.

The "Paper Wall" Legal Trust

Julian Croft (Lead Vocals) and Maya Sterling (Percussion) live as a married couple but remain legally single. Under current disability laws, marriage would strip Julian of his SSI and Medicaid—a death sentence for his care.

Engine Room Records does not just distribute their music. We fund the "Paper Wall" legal trust that protects their assets and independence—and gave the band its permanent name.

The "Safe Harbor" Lineup

  • Julian Croft ("Leo")
    Lead Vocals / Composition
  • Maya Sterling ("Olivia")
    Percussion / Vocals / Care Partner
  • The Sisters (Luna, Stella, Charlie): Izzy, Bea, Charlotte Croft
  • The Cousins (Enforcers): Diana Hale, Ellie Cross, Fiona Croft

Archive: The Meeting

DATE: OCTOBER 2000
LOC: CPI CAMPUS / KINCAID HALL

Julian Croft was 19, attempting to restart his life after escaping his abuser ("Vanessa"). He rolled into the back of Kincaid Hall during a CPI Orientation event, unsure if he belonged.

On stage, Ryan O'Connell—The Stardust Engine's T10 paraplegic frontman—was strapped into his chair, sweating, screaming, and dominating the room with the band's anthem, Ignition (The Forger's Call).

Julian watched Ryan command 60,000 "Ironheads" without standing up. He watched the O'Connell siblings and Wright twins operate as a single, protective unit.

Julian grabbed Maya's hand. He realized he didn't need to be "cured" to be on stage. He turned to her and said:
"We're going to build an engine, too."

Corporate Provenance: The 2004–2015 Diversification

When The Stardust Engine commissioned their 2002 Sainte-Claire 45H3 and 2004 Prairie Coachworks RLFD30, both coaches were originally purchased cash-in-full by Engine Room Records, LLC—which at the time served as the family's single all-purpose operating company.

After the band signed off at the conclusion of 2004's Progress Street to recover from severe touring burnout, CEO Holly O'Connell spent the 2004–2015 hiatus systematically unbundling the label into a fortress of specialized entities. Realizing that a single highway accident involving a 45,000-pound motorcoach could expose the band's master recordings to catastrophic litigation, Holly spun off the physical properties and heavy fleet into Stardust Strategic Assets, LLC (a subsidiary of Stardust Properties, LLC), completing the anonymous corporate web in the 2015 Delaware Migration.

The Interstate Fortress (60-Inch Vertical Hydraulic Lift)

Commissioned on March 14, 2002, during the band's sold-out Trans-Canada Tour in Montréal, "The Iron Horse" is a ground-up custom 45-foot high-deck tri-axle entertainer coach built by Sainte-Claire Coachworks in Québec.

Because a high-deck interstate cruiser places the main living floor 60 inches above the pavement to accommodate massive underfloor luggage and equipment bays, Ryan O'Connell could not board via a conventional ramp. Holly O'Connell presented the Québécois engineering team—in flawless French—with structural schematics for a 400-pound commercial hydraulic cassette platform lift integrated directly into a full-height mid-ship accessibility door.

Impressed by the family's humility and engineering rigor (and disgusted by an American pop star demanding a rooftop Jacuzzi that compromised frame rigidity), Sainte-Claire's VP of Sales moved The Stardust Engine to Bay 1. Wrapped in the band's signature Cosmic Nebula violet, cyan, and amber stardust livery over Obsidian Midnight paint, The Iron Horse gave Ryan total autonomy across North America's interstates.

While the 45-foot Sainte-Claire 45H3 was built to cross continents, maneuvering a towering tri-axle highway liner down tight residential streets like Progress Street NE or through the campus turns of Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI)—and waiting several minutes to deploy a heavy 60-inch vertical hydraulic lift for a quick local trip—was impractical.

In early 2004, while recording their homecoming album Progress Street, The Stardust Engine became the very first launch customer for Prairie Coachworks' newly restyled 30-foot low-floor platform: the 2004 RLFD30 (Restyled Low-Floor Diesel, 30-Foot).

Built as a single-door executive day-coach (deleting the rear transit exit door in favor of continuous dark-tinted acoustic lounge glass), the RLFD30 uses pneumatic kneeling suspension and a simple front flip-out aluminum ADA ramp. Inspired by the family's fond memories of riding Blue Ridge Transit's Route 1 along Main Street and Progress Street during their CPI student years, Ryan can roll straight off the Blacksburg sidewalk and into the cabin in five seconds flat.

Because The Stardust Engine signed on as the official Launch Customer (Serial #001) for Prairie Coachworks' restyled 30-foot low-floor platform before the first municipal transit orders were even delivered, the manufacturer issued the following press release on Delivery Day. Ryan, Cassidy, Holly, Evan, and Tyler keep a framed copy mounted on the forward bulkhead just behind the driver's cockpit—and carry laminated copies in the glovebox to show fellow transit enthusiasts on the road.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE — MAY 18, 2004 PRAIRIE COACHWORKS, INC. // SPECIALTY & EXECUTIVE TRANSIT DIVISION

PRAIRIE COACHWORKS UNVEILS RESTYLED 2004 RLFD30 LOW-FLOOR PLATFORM; DELIVERS SERIAL #001 LAUNCH COACH TO INDEPENDENT ROCK ACT "THE STARDUST ENGINE"

First-of-its-kind 30-foot Restyled Low-Floor Diesel (RLFD30) single-door executive coach pairs heavy-duty urban transit accessibility with custom acoustic touring architecture for Blacksburg, Virginia musicians.

WINNIPEG, MB & BLACKSBURG, VA (May 18, 2004) — Prairie Coachworks, Inc. today announced the official commercial launch and first customer delivery of its all-new 2004 RLFD30 (Restyled Low-Floor Diesel, 30-Foot) heavy-duty coach platform. In an industry first, Serial #001 of the restyled low-floor line has been delivered not to a metropolitan transit authority, but to Virginia-based independent rock band The Stardust Engine and their operating label, Engine Room Records, LLC, who serve as the global Launch Customer for the RLFD30 program.

Engineered on Prairie Coachworks' newly restyled aerodynamic front and rear fiberglass masks with roof-integrated HVAC fairings, the 30-foot rigid monocoque chassis was developed for tight university corridors and historic downtown street grids where 40-foot and 60-foot coaches cannot easily maneuver. Working directly with Engine Room Records Chief Executive Officer Holly O'Connell, Prairie Coachworks' Specialty Vehicles Engineering Group created a bespoke Front-Door-Only Executive Configuration—deleting the standard rear exit door to form a continuous, studio-insulated acoustic lounge with flush-mounted frameless dark-tinted panoramic glass.

At the core of Serial #001's mission is uncompromising, zero-delay accessibility for frontman and lead guitarist Ryan O'Connell, who has used a manual wheelchair since surviving a 1990 highway collision. By combining Prairie Coachworks' fast-acting pneumatic front-axle kneeling suspension with an integrated heavy-gauge aluminum flip-out ADA boarding ramp, the RLFD30 lowers its entrance threshold directly to the sidewalk curb—allowing O'Connell to roll from pavement to cabin unassisted in under five seconds.

"When Holly and Ryan O'Connell approached us with their specifications, they didn't ask for rock-star vanity—they asked for transit-grade reliability, structural integrity, and five-second curb autonomy on the streets of Blacksburg. Having a band of former Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute commuters christen Serial #001 of the RLFD30—complete with factory-programmed Luminator Horizon amber LED headsigns reading PROGRESS STREET and THE STARDUST ENGINE—is the proudest launch in our division's history."

Marc-André Beaulieu, Vice President of Engineering & Specialty Coaches, Prairie Coachworks, Inc.

In another milestone for the Winnipeg delivery center, The Stardust Engine became the first private customer in Prairie Coachworks history to dispatch three of its own principals—CEO Holly O'Connell, bassist Evan Wright, and drummer Tyler Wright—all holding valid Class A Commercial Driver's Licenses (CDL) with full Passenger (P) and Airbrake endorsements, to personally execute the factory road-test inspection and pilot Serial #001 home to Montgomery County, Virginia.

"In college, riding the low-floor campus buses down Main Street and Progress Street was how my sisters, my cousins, and I got our independence back after the crash. Being the launch customer for the 2004 RLFD30 means that wherever we pull up to the curb, the ramp flips out in five seconds and we're home. We're prouder of this 30-foot bus than any platinum plaque on the wall."

Ryan O'Connell, Lead Vocalist & Guitarist, The Stardust Engine
### END RELEASE // PRAIRIE COACHWORKS ARCHIVE SERIAL #2004-RLFD30-001 ###
Post-1990 Security & Safety Mandate

The CDL Protocol: Why No Outsider Ever Drives the Bus

Following the December 10, 1990 crash on Interstate 81 that left Ryan O'Connell with a complete T10 spinal cord injury, the family instituted an unbreakable operational rule: no hired commercial driver would ever hold their lives in their hands again.

Before taking delivery of heavy coaches, Holly O'Connell, Evan Wright, and Tyler Wright all completed commercial heavy-vehicle training and earned their Class A Commercial Driver's Licenses (CDL) with full Passenger (P) and Airbrake endorsements. The Narrative Timeline

The fictional history of Engine Room Records.

1987: Electric Color

APEX RECORDS // THE GILDED CAGE

The Stardust Engine exploded into the mainstream with their 1987 debut, Electric Color. The title track was a massive, studio-mandated synth-pop hit, sitting at the #2 spot for six weeks. While fans embraced it, the band viewed this era as the beginning of a "Cold War" with Apex Records.

The studio constantly prioritized polished, radio-friendly production over the band's authentic rock roots. Tracks like "Dancing in the Neon" kept the lights on, but Ryan began hiding angsty, anti-corporate lyrics inside the safe pop wrappers ("Plastic Sky") in an act of malicious compliance.

Access Album Archive

1989: Neon Hearts

APEX RECORDS // THE SIDE B REBELLION

For their 1989 sophomore album, Neon Hearts, Apex Records demanded pure brand consistency. Terrified by industry controversy, the executives demanded an absurdly short, manic 1:54 bubblegum pop track ("Side by Side") to ensure the album felt "safe."

But the fans were catching on. When Apex begrudgingly allowed a "one-two punch" of pure rock on Side B ("Chain Reaction" and "Not Your Doll"), the tracks became immediate fan-favorites. It was definitive proof that the heavier "Engine" sound was exactly what the audience wanted, setting the stage for the coming war.

Access Album Archive

1990: Live in Chicago

APEX RECORDS // THE SABOTAGED SHOW

During the Neon Hearts tour, the band was squeezed into a strict 30-minute opening slot. The resulting live album is a source of fury for the band; the mix was actively sabotaged by Apex Records, maliciously burying Cassidy's "Stardust" synth leitmotif deep into the background to rebrand them as a male-fronted rock act.

However, the recording serves as the historical "Smoking Gun" that later dismantled the label's corporate narrative. During the opening, Ryan explicitly introduces Cassidy to the crowd as "my sister," publicly disproving the studio executive's assumption that they were a married couple.

Access Album Archive

1990: The Crash of '90

INTERSTATE 81 // THE NIGHT THE ENGINE BROKE

On December 10, 1990, racing a winter storm back to Blacksburg on Interstate 81, their Holt Freighter touring van was clipped by a speeding sedan. The van spun off the icy road and rolled into the embankment.

While the rest of the family sustained minor injuries, Ryan O'Connell was pinned. He suffered a complete T10 spinal cord injury, losing all function and sensation below the waist. The subsequent year was a brutal hiatus focused entirely on survival, establishing strict medical protocols as the band prepared for their eventual, defiant return.

Access Full Declassified Archive

1992: The "Friction" Catastrophe

LOS ANGELES, CA // THE DECLARATION OF INDEPENDENCE

In September 1992, the "Cold War" culminated in a disastrous Los Angeles photo shoot for their canceled sophomore album, Friction. Executive Julian Vance misinterpreted Cassidy's concept art (a space shuttle experiencing orbital friction) and assumed the siblings were a married couple, attempting to coerce them into a highly inappropriate marketing campaign.

The band's 23-year-old manager, Holly O'Connell, recognized the demands as a severe breach of contract. A police intervention turned the dispute into a legal scandal. Apex Records completely surrendered, voided the contract, returned all master tapes, and paid a massive settlement. Holly used this capital to establish Engine Room Records.

Access Full Declassified Archive

1992-1994: The Blacksburg Exile

BLACKSBURG, VA // LOS ANGELES, CA

Following the collapse of the Friction project, the band immediately evacuated Los Angeles, retreating 2,500 miles back to their sanctuary in Blacksburg, Virginia.

Meanwhile, Holly O'Connell remained on the West Coast to dismantle Apex Records. In a media circus rivaling the "Trial of the Century," Julian Vance faced criminal and civil trials. He was found guilty on all charges, and the judge ruled decisively in the band's favor in civil court. Desperate to stop the PR bleeding, Apex Records capitulated to all of Holly's demands, returning their master tapes and copyrights, which she used to formally establish Engine Room Records, LLC. The trauma and isolation of these "Wilderness Years" became a creative crucible for the band in Blacksburg.

Era Documented in friction Archive

1995: The Warehouse Tapes

BLACKSBURG, VA // THE INDEPENDENT ERA BEGINS

In 1995, Engine Room Records launched its first official release. Operating entirely outside the traditional music industry ecosystem, the family fulfilled mail-orders directly to their loyal "Ironhead" fanbase.

The album itself was a sonic exorcism. Side A featured raw, unpolished rock tracks (such as "Static" and "Garbage") that explicitly rejected the manufactured synth-pop forced upon them by Apex Records, while simultaneously tearing down the exhausting "victim" narrative pushed by the tabloid media.

Access Album Archive

1996: The "American Dream"

DALEVILLE, VA // THE BILLION-DOLLAR PARADIGM SHIFT

Engine Room Records had proven it could survive independently, but in 1996, a completely random event transformed the label from a self-sustaining warehouse operation into an unassailable financial juggernaut.

Cassidy O'Connell purchased a "Quick Pick" ticket for the American Dream lottery. She allowed the machine to select the numbers, keeping the ticket simply because she liked the geometric pattern they formed on the slip. That single ticket was the sole winner of a historic $2.04 Billion annuitized jackpot.

The family opted for the lump-sum payout in absolute privacy. Holly immediately established the Forger Nation Trust to manage the wealth, weaponizing the capital to purchase state-of-the-art logistics fleets and infrastructure for Engine Room Records.

Classified Corporate Operations

1996: Escape Velocity (Ad Astra)

GLOBAL RETAIL // THE BREAKTHROUGH SINGLE

Originally conceptualized as the B-Side of The Warehouse Tapes, this 15-minute progressive rock magnum opus was elevated to a monumental A-Side EP release in 1996. Financed by their newly secured independence, this release officially ended their "Wilderness Years."

Knowing mainstream radio would never play a 15-minute suite, Manager Holly O'Connell cut a condensed 5-minute "Trojan Horse" edit. By stripping away the ambient transitions and focusing on the core narrative arc, this strategic edit successfully charted, introducing millions of new fans to the band's independent sound.

Access Album Archive

1997: Hard Reset

GLOBAL RETAIL // THE $13.99 OFFENSIVE

In 1997, The Stardust Engine released Hard Reset. This massive, two-disc progressive rock epic was Engine Room Records' first foray into traditional commercial distribution. Holly O'Connell set the retail price for the double-album at a staggering $13.99, accomplishing this by weaponizing the Forger Nation Trust's risk-free U.S. Treasury yields to subsidize manufacturing.

Terrified by this market disruption, a coalition of major labels—led by Apex Records—filed a massive antitrust injunction. Holly dismantled their coalition in federal court, proving it was simply a superior, privately funded business model. The injunction was dismissed, and Hard Reset dominated the global charts.

Access Album Archive

1998: The First Signing

ENGINE ROOM RECORDS // FRACTURED PRISMS

With The Stardust Engine securely established as a self-sustaining entity, Holly O'Connell began expanding the fortress. In 1998, Engine Room Records signed their very first external act: a reclusive British synth-pop duo named Fractured Prisms.

The band had been dropped by their old label and their back catalog was out of print. Using her immense financial leverage, Holly ruthlessly acquired Fractured Prisms's entire catalog and offered the siblings a secure, uncompromising place to land and record music again.

1999: Fractured Prisms Debut

ENGINE ROOM RECORDS // CARNABY STREET

In 1999, Engine Room Records proudly re-released Fractured Prisms's self-titled debut album (unofficially known to fans as Carnaby Street due to its iconic album art). The re-release resurrected the "lost" masterpiece of 1983, allowing a new generation to discover the haunting, atmospheric synth-pop that had defined an era.

Under the protective banner of Engine Room Records, Rhys and Claire were finally given the creative freedom and financial backing to begin work on their massive concept album, a rock opera detailing their intricate 1883 narrative lore.

2001: Midnight Drivers

THE VAULT // THE LOST 1987 SESSIONS

In 2001, Engine Room Records independently resurrected and released Midnight Drivers. Because the title track was the only song actually written during the fraught 1987 sessions, the band had to build an entire retro-engineered album around it from scratch in 2001.

Side A acts as an explosive, high-speed synth-pop prologue. This brilliant pacing sets the stage for a vibrant night out in the city, allowing the raw, untouched 1987 master of the title track to open Side B with maximum impact. It pulls the listener out of the bright lights and directly into the dark, finding sanctuary in a moving car at night.

Destination Dispatch

Smart Grouping. Reduced Wait Times. Universal Access.

How it Works

Unlike traditional elevators where you press a button inside the car, Destination Dispatch asks you to select your floor at a kiosk before you board. The system groups passengers going to the same floors together, reducing the number of stops and making your ride faster.

Standard Operation

01
Select

Approach the touchscreen kiosk in the lobby. Type your floor number manually OR tap your building badge.

02
Assign

The screen will display a letter (e.g., "A", "B"). This is your assigned elevator.

03
Board

Walk to the door labeled with your letter. There are no floor buttons inside the car. It will take you automatically.

Smart Badge Integration

For employees and frequent visitors, we offer a "Home Floor" programming feature. This allows for a predictable, nearly touchless experience while maintaining flexibility for neurodivergent needs.

NFC TAP & WAIT

The "Decision Window" Workflow
  1. Tap Your Badge: Hold your card to the reader.
  2. The Pause: The screen displays your name and default floor (e.g., Floor 39). The system pauses for 3–5 seconds.
  3. Automatic Selection: If you do nothing, it confirms your home floor and assigns a car.
  4. The Pivot: During the pause, you can manually tap a different floor (e.g., Floor 40 - Quiet Floor) if you need a sensory break instead of going to your office.

Accessibility & Neuro-Inclusion

The Accessibility Button

Located on every kiosk. Pressing this physical button activates "ADA Mode," which triggers:

  • Audio Guidance: Voice instructions for visually impaired users.
  • Extended Dwell: Doors stay open longer for safe boarding.
  • Priority Assignment: Assigns an elevator with more space/fewer passengers.
Cognitive Safety

Destination Dispatch reduces social anxiety and sensory overload by design:

  • Predictability: You know your car assignment before you board. No rushing to find buttons in a crowd.
  • Reduced Crowding: Smart grouping means fewer stops and a quieter ride.
What if I get on the wrong elevator?
If you board the wrong car, do not panic. Simply exit at the next available stop. Every lobby has a kiosk where you can re-enter your destination.
Can I hold the door?
Please do not hold the doors. The system calculates weight and timing precisely to optimize flow. Blocking the sensor may cause the elevator to go out of service. Another car will be assigned immediately.
